articles.title: Rahm Emanuel urges Democrats to pass stock trading ban, give Washington a 'house cleaning'
articles.summary: Rahm Emanuel calls on Democrats to ban lawmaker stock trading and pass sweeping ethics reform in 2027, warning party leaders that investigations alone will not satisfy voters.
articles.body: Former White House chief of staff Rahm Emanuel is calling on Democrats to make a ban on stock trading across all three branches of government a top legislative priority. Speaking on "Fox & Friends," Wednesday, Emanuel urged his party to turn investigations into legislative action, arguing lawmakers must pass a sweeping ethics bill in 2027 that would prohibit officials in all three branches of government from buying and selling individual stocks. "Pass a comprehensive ethics bill for all three branches," Emanuel said, arguing that investigations alone are "not the change alone that the American people voted for." RAHM EMANUEL LAYS OUT FIVE-POINT ETHICS PLAN, SAYS DEMOCRATS SHOULD LEARN FROM GOP-LED STATES ON EDUCATION Emanuel, who has floated a 2028 presidential run, said the package should also prohibit officials from betting on prediction markets, ban stock trading, mandate blind trusts, impose term limits or a mandatory retirement age, and restrict foreign income during and after government service. "The way I look at this election is pretty straightforward. It was a repudiation of President Trump, Project [20]25 and the Republicans. When you look at how deep and how broad this is, it's very clear. But what the Democrats do in 2027 will determine whether we have won," he said. RAHM EMANUEL PLEADS FOR THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY TO WELCOME MORE 'MCCAIN-ROMNEY REPUBLICANS' "I am for following the money. Where did all this money go? Who got these contracts? But it has to lead to ethics and lobbying reform legislation," Emanuel added. Senate Democrats previously blocked a Republican-backed effort to address stock trading by lawmakers. The Stop Insider Trading Act passed the House in July, despite opposition from a majority of House Democrats. Democrats argued that the proposed restrictions on stock trading did not go far enough and objected to a photo voter ID provision included in the legislation. SCHUMER TANKS POPULAR INSIDER TRADING BAN IN DEM EFFORT TO DERAIL REPUBLICAN'S AGENDA AHEAD OF MIDTERMS Emanuel argued that passing comprehensive ethics legislation could help Democrats maintain support from moderate Republicans who backed the party in the midterm elections. "There is time now for all of Washington to get a good house cleaning and scrubbing," Emanuel said. RAHM EMANUEL CHALLENGES DSA’S INFLUENCE ON DEMOCRATS, WARNS GOP ‘WING’ IS DISAPPEARING When pressed on his political future and whether he would enter the 2028 Democratic presidential race, Emanuel predicted voters would see "31 flavors" of candidates and offered a playful description of his potential place in the field. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "In 2028, my prediction is you're going to have a Baskin-Robbins, 31 flavors. And if I decide to do this, I'm [going to] be Rocky Road," he said, adding that he would "tell you the truth, whether you [want to] hear it or not."

articles.title: Hakeem Jeffries touts historic midterm victories
articles.summary: "The American people have chosen House Democrats because they want to see a dramatic change in direction," Jeffries said.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries , D-N.Y., touted Democrats' historic midterm wins on Wednesday, calling them "a great victory for the American people."

"The American people have chosen House Democrats because they want to see a dramatic change in direction," Jeffries said at a press conference. "And that's exactly what House Democrats will deliver. Beginning on day one."

Jeffries, Clark could make history as House majority leaders

This comes as Democrats are projected to take control of both chambers of Congress, with Jeffries poised to make history as the first Black Speaker of the House. He'll face a vote of his colleagues when the new Congress convenes on Jan. 3.

Jeffries was joined onstage by House Minority Whip Katherine Clark, D-Mass., and House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar. Clark could also make history as the first woman to serve as House majority leader.

Midterm outcomes represent 'stunning rebuke of MAGA extremism': Jeffries

While Jeffries said the midterm outcomes represent a "stunning rebuke of MAGA extremism," he added that the new Congress will "fight hard for every single American wherever you may reside."

Jeffries also noted Democrats are "ready, willing and able" to work across the aisle, but that he hasn't heard from President Donald Trump so far.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump brags about the White House ballroom in his first post-election appearance
articles.summary: In his first public appearance since Republicans racked up major losses in the midterm elections, President Donald Trump boasted Wednesday about the White House ballroom under construction and largely skirted talk about his party’s performance.
articles.body: In his first public appearance since Republicans racked up major losses in the midterm elections, President Donald Trump boasted Wednesday about the White House ballroom under construction and largely skirted talk about his party’s performance. “This is a special structure. It’s going to be not only one of the biggest, but it’ll be the most beautiful ballroom, I think, anywhere in the world, and they’ve been trying to get it for 150 years,” Trump told construction workers at the ballroom site on the White House grounds, where the East Wing previously stood. “This will be something very special. And so we’re putting up the last piece of steel. I thought it would be appropriate to have the media here,” he added, hinting that the ballroom’s “official opening” would be in the near future. The president’s only remarks on the election results — which saw Democrats regain control of both houses of Congress, notching wins in longtime GOP strongholds like Texas — came in response to questions from the media after his remarks. When asked to weigh in on the race to pick a new House Republican leader in light of Speaker Mike Johnson’s decision not to run again, Trump said, “We’ll stay out of it.” He said he did not ask Johnson to step down. Asked for comment on Vice President JD Vance’s statement that Republicans lost the election because of the war on Iran, Trump said, “I think it’s largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term.” He added: “At the same time, if I had it to do again, I’d have to do it again because long term it’s the only answer. You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon.” The president signed a steel beam destined for the ballroom project, adorned with two gold presidential seals, and addressed criticism that he is too focused on White House renovations. “I’m doing it because the White House is the ultimate symbol of America and it’s got to be pristine — it’s got to be perfect,” he said. “And if you take a look at it, that’s what it is right now. You have no idea how much work we had to do.” Trump claimed that it was “the dream of presidents to have a ballroom for 150 years” and bragged about the “most beautiful marble” in the ballroom. “I got it for the floor of the ballroom at the White House. And it’s going to be beautiful. The walls are going to be very — you’ll see a lot of glass,” he said. Trump first announced plans for the ballroom in July 2025 and has frequently spoken about it during official White House events on unrelated subjects and at campaign rallies. The project has faced legal obstacles, though the Supreme Court said in late August that construction could proceed indefinitely. On Monday, Trump spent most of his final pre-election speech in front of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool touting the renovations he ordered around Washington, D.C., with very little time devoted to the midterms.

articles.title: House Dem who defied Hakeem Jeffries scores upset win in pro-Trump district
articles.summary: Marie Gluesenkamp Perez ran a heated race against John Braun in a district Donald Trump carried in 2024.
articles.body: A Democratic lawmaker who publicly defied House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., twice beat the odds to win re-election in a district that President Donald Trump carried in 2024. Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, D-Wash., defeated Republican Washington State Sen. John Braun to win a third term in the House of Representatives, The Associated Press reported. It's an important victory for House Democrats in their quest to claw back the majority in Congress, but one that could also create drama for party leaders on key votes over the next two years. JEFFRIES THREATENS 'SERIOUS RESPONSE' AFTER DEMOCRATS HELP GOP ADVANCE ANTI-SOCIALISM VOTE Gluesenkamp Perez, who has been known to buck her party on votes in the past, infuriated her fellow Democrats twice in September when she sided with Republicans on procedural votes that helped GOP leaders rescue their agenda from conservative rebellions. If not for her and Rep. Jared Golden, D-Maine, siding with Republicans on those two votes, the House GOP's agenda would have been paralyzed. The first time earned her a rare public rebuke from Jeffries, who called it a "breach of trust." Other left-wing lawmakers called for her to be removed from the powerful House Appropriations Committee over the move. But one could argue that Gluesenkamp Perez's public defiance of her own party was critical for her political survival. Trump won her district by roughly 3 percentage points in 2024, and she first won her seat by defeating an incumbent House Republican. Washington's 3rd Congressional District includes rural areas and the city of Vancouver, and smaller coastal towns in the southwest portion of the state. He was later named Trump's director of the United States National Counterterrorism Center, but resigned over disagreements on Middle East policy. articles.title: George Santos on midterm elections: It’s a s‑‑‑ show
articles.summary: Former Rep. George Santos (R-N.Y.) called the midterm elections a “s‑‑‑ show” for Republicans following major GOP losses in key Senate and House races. “Repu...
articles.body:
Former Rep. George Santos (R-N.Y.) called the midterm elections a "s‑‑‑ show" for Republicans following major GOP losses in key Senate and House races.

"Republicans literally squandered their majority. Congratulations," he told TMZ DC's Jacob Wasserman. "We have people losing seats in states that we never thought we'd see, like Ann Wagner lost Missouri. Not that I'm going to cry over that. I might celebrate and go drink some champagne right now. But the point I'm trying to make is, it's a disaster. It's a f‑‑‑ing disaster. It's a full f‑‑‑ing disaster."

"Imagine if it rained knives for a month and then that turned into a wave. That's what happened tonight. Ashley Hinson can't win Iowa. It's just a s‑‑‑ show," the former lawmaker expressed, adding that the results "absolutely scares the s‑‑‑ out of" him "for what happens next."

Santos was referencing Democrat Josh Turek's defeat of Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) in Iowa's competitive Senate election. The state has been considered a Republican stronghold, but Hinson's loss — alongside the GOP's defeat in the state's gubernatorial election — has swung it to the Democratic Party.

In Texas, James Talarico became the first member of the Democratic Party to win a Texas Senate seat in decades, defeating state Attorney General Ken Paxton (R). Though Republicans held on to seats in Florida, Democrats picked up other key seats in Michigan and Kansas.

In the interview, Santos also withdrew his pitch to become the next White House press secretary, citing Tuesday's election results.

"I love the president, but no, I'm good," he said. "Today was a bad night. Everybody has bad nights, and I had a notoriously bad night that everybody saw."

When asked if he had any advice for incoming congressional members, Santos echoed a post from Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.): "Lawyer up."

Garcia is also the incoming chair for the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee.

articles.title: Carlos Cuerpo toma su primera decisión al frente de Transportes tras sustituir a Óscar Puente: cesa al presidente de Adif
articles.standfirst: El nuevo ministro releva a Luis Pedro Marco de la Peña en su primera gran decisión tras la crisis ferroviaria de Urda
articles.summary: El nuevo ministro releva a Luis Pedro Marco de la Peña en su primera gran decisión tras la crisis ferroviaria de Urda
articles.body: El vicepresidente primero del Gobierno ha decidido apartar a Luis Pedro Marco de la Peña de la presidencia de Adif después de mantener una reunión con él y con el secretario de Estado de Transportes, José Antonio Santano. El cese se produce en un momento de especial tensión para el sector ferroviario, marcado por las consecuencias del accidente de Urda y las críticas a la gestión de la seguridad en la red. Carlos Cuerpo ha asumido temporalmente las competencias del Ministerio de Transportes tras la dimisión de Óscar Puente. El anterior ministro comunicó su salida después de comparecer en la Diputación Permanente para dar explicaciones sobre la tragedia ferroviaria, que dejó 69 fallecidos, y abordar las circunstancias que rodearon el siniestro. Marco de la Peña había sido convocado por Cuerpo para explicar el siniestro y trasladar la información disponible. Su continuidad estaba en cuestión desde la dimisión de Puente, anunciada durante su comparecencia en la Diputación Permanente. La oposición y varios sindicatos habían reclamado responsabilidades en Adif. El ya expresidente llegó al cargo el 17 de septiembre de 2024, en sustitución de Ángel Contreras. Ingeniero de Caminos, trabajó en empresas privadas y ocupó responsabilidades en el área de Transportes del Gobierno vasco. Su salida se produce tras dos accidentes ferroviarios en la red de alta velocidad. La reunión también contó con Santano, número dos de Puente. Cuerpo agradeció al presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, la confianza para asumir “esta enorme responsabilidad”, con la memoria de las víctimas “muy presente”. Sánchez destacó su “capacidad de gestión, integridad y talante”. La nueva etapa deberá afrontar la pérdida de confianza en el ferrocarril y aplicar medidas para reforzar la seguridad. Entre ellas figuran reducir las frecuencias en el corredor Madrid-Sevilla, aumentar la distancia entre trenes y supervisar las comunicaciones entre los centros de control y los maquinistas. La investigación continúa abierta por el momento.

articles.title: How major demographic swings propelled Democrats to a midterm rout
articles.summary: Huge double-digit swings among young, Latino and first-time voters toward Democrats helped fuel a blue tsunami in the midterm election.
articles.body:
WASHINGTON — Democrats pulled off a stunning midterm rout by making sizable inroads with nearly every major demographic as Americans delivered one of the most resounding midterm rebukes in modern U.S. history.

The outcome marked about a 15-point national swing toward Democrats from the 2024 election, led by significant double-digit shifts among young, Latino and first-time voters — groups that President Donald Trump had made notable inroads with in the 2024 election.

Democrats won Hispanic voters by a 62%-35% margin nationally ‒ a 22-point swing after Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris won the cohort 51%-46% in the 2024 election.

Midterm voters younger than 30 years old backed Democrats by a whopping 72%-25% spread ‒ a 36-point swing after Trump only lost the group by 11 percentage points in 2024. The swing was most pronounced among young men under 30, who voted for Democrats 66%-31% after Trump carried young men in 2024 by a 49%-48% margin.

Voters who cast their ballots for the first time in the midterm election backed Democrats 64%-34% ‒ a 41-point swing after Trump won first-time voters 55%-44% in the 2024 election.

Figures are according to exit-poll data taken by the Associated Press in conjunction with the five major television networks , compared to exit polls in the 2024 election.

It was an unmistakable repudiation of Trump's second term.

Fueled by these and other significant demographic shifts, Democrats scored upset wins across the country, flipping at least seven Republican-held Senate seats, including in traditionally Republican states such as Texas, Kansas, Iowa and South Carolina. Texas hadn't elected a Democratic U.S. senator since 1988; and Kansas not since 1932, when Hebert Hoover was president.

Democrats have a chance to widen their Senate majority further with potential victories in Mississippi and Alaska ‒ two other reliably red states where Democrats are clinging to slim leads as votes are still being counted. Democrats also took control of the House of Representatives, flipping at least 35 seats previously held by Republicans, including in districts that Trump carried by more than 20 percentage points.

The shellacking for Republicans was across the board.

Americans who lack college degrees ‒ the backbone of Trump's MAGA base ‒ backed Republicans by only a four-point-margin, 51%-47%, in this year's midterms. It was a 9-point shift toward Democrats after Trump won non-college educated voters 56%-43% in 2024.

Democrats won college-educated voters ‒ a recent stronghold for the party ‒ by a 62%-36% margin. The 26-point difference was a swing of 12 percentage points toward Democrats from the 2024 election.

Amid concerns about the rising cost of living, Americans who earn $50,000 or less voted for Democrats 57%-41% ‒ a sizable 18-point shift after Trump won the same group 50%-48% in 2024. Democrats also won among voters who earn more than $100,000 by 12 percentage points, an 8-point swing after they won this group by four percentage points in 2024.

Longtime pollster Frank Luntz said most voters who went from casting ballots for Trump in 2024 to voting for Democrats in the midterms had one thing in common: they felt misled by Trump's campaign promise to lower costs.

"They felt disappointed and just disillusioned with what's happened over the past two years, specifically over affordability," Luntz said, pointing to findings in a focus group he conducted of Republican midterm voters from key battleground states. "They all ‒ no matter what part of the country they were from ‒ complained about how high prices had gotten and how they had been promised lower prices."

By far, the top midterm issue was the the economy, with 39% of voters calling it the most important issue facing the country, followed by the state of democracy at 32%, and immigration at 11%.

Male voters broke even in the midterms, with Democrats and Republicans getting support from 49% of men after Trump won male voters by a dozen percentage points in 2024. Democrats won female voters in the midterms by 18 percentage points, 58%-40% ‒ a shift of 10 points toward Democrats from 2024.

After losing Catholic voters by 20 percentage points in 2024, Democrats only lost them by 2 percentage points in the midterms. Republicans still won voters who identify as Protestant Christians by a wide 22 percentage points, but was a closer margin than the 27-point differential in the 2024 election.

One of the only demographics that shifted away from Democrats appeared to be Jewish voters. Though Jewish voters backed Democrats 68%-31% in the midterms, Harris won Jewish voters 78%-22% over Trump in the 2024 election. The shift comes as Israel's war in Gaza and U.S. military support for Israel have increasingly become galvanizing issue within the Democratic Party.

And despite the big night for Democrats, only 47% of midterm voters said they had a favorable opinion of the Democratic Party.

"This is no endorsement of the Democratic Party or the Democratic agenda," Luntz added. "It was rejection on what happened, or more importantly what didn't happen, over the last two years."

articles.title: As GOP points fingers over stunning midterm losses, Trump admires his ballroom
articles.summary: The president sounded almost sanguine when discussing construction progress.
articles.body:
In the midst of the GOP reckoning with massive losses in the midterms, President Donald Trump on Wednesday hastily called the press in to cover his first public remarks from the White House since the Democrats overwhelmingly wrestled control of both the House and Senate.

But for 20 minutes, the president didn't address the history-making renouncement of his administration that voters delivered Tuesday night. Instead, the president, standing in the construction site of the White House ballroom in front of a large beam, spoke to a crowd of construction workers about his many passion projects to "beautify Washington" — first and foremost, the massive ballroom befit with 50-foot ceilings and the capacity to hold hundreds of guests.

"This will be the ballroom. Right here is the ballroom. Over here, you're going to have magnificent columns on this side, outside exterior columns, very much like the Supreme Court. They're actually taller and they're even more magnificent," Trump said.

An almost sanguine sounding Trump ticked through a progress report of the various construction projects underway as he looks to remake Washington in his image. It was a sharp contrast from Republicans nationwide — Trump's defeated 2024 primary foe Ron DeSantis' first public remarks called the midterms an " extinction-level event for Republicans " — who are grasping for lessons learned and a way forward after a Tuesday night beatdown.

"I love construction," the president said, before turning around and putting his signature on the last of the ballroom's beams, in thick black sharpie.

As political strategists delivered their autopsies of the midterm results in lengthy X posts and GOP finger-pointing unfolded with fervor, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, the president's right-hand-man on construction projects around the city, stood before the crowd and declared Wednesday "a day of celebration" and "a day of gratitude."

"This is the last beam that's going into place," Burgum said. "It's going to be raised up, and that's what we're here to celebrate."

Trump made clear that the decision to focus on the construction project on Wednesday was his idea.

"I thought the press should be here. This was a non-press event," Trump said, amid some amicable small talk in front of a group of photographers. "I said 'this is the greatest, right?'"

Wednesday's site tour — accompanied by handshakes and signing hardhats for construction workers — was a world away from the last time he faced a midterm drubbing in 2018. That time, he called an angry press conference berating Republicans and blaming them for their losses.

"Mia Love gave me no love. And she lost. Too bad," Trump said eight years ago, referencing the then-battleground Utah Republican.

Wednesday's event echoed the president's last public remarks before the midterms, when he closed the cycle with a speech before the Reflecting Pool on the National Mall, an embattled project to repaint the shallow water feature in front of the monument to Abraham Lincoln.

The midterms only came up after the president delivered remarks, at the prompting of the press.

After taking a few questions about Speaker Mike Johnson stepping down from his post after Tuesday's losses, and Vice President JD Vance's assertion that his party lost so handily because of the war in Iran that the president championed, Trump calmly directed the attention back to the ballroom.

"Now watch the beam go up," he said, as the hunk of metal carrying his signature was hoisted into its place in the ceiling.

"Now envision chandeliers all over your ceiling. Envision marble floor. Oh, it's going to be beautiful. This will be the most beautiful building," the president said.

articles.title: Abortion, transgender rights and voter ID: Ballot measure results from the 2026 midterms
articles.summary: Ballot measures voters a way to directly alter their state laws, rather than relying solely on legislators to create policy on their behalf.
articles.body:
The battle for control of Congress got the lion's share of the attention on Tuesday, but there were a lot of other consequential measures on the ballots that could have a direct impact on voters' lives.

Ballot measures often don't receive much national focus, but every two years, voters across the country decide whether to adopt policies that have major implications for their states. This year was no different.

There were more than 140 measures on the ballot across 40 states. Many touched on some of the biggest issues in U.S. politics, including abortion, transgender rights, voting and the democratic process itself.

Ballot measures can give the people a way to directly alter the laws in their states instead of relying solely on their elected representatives to create policy on their behalf. In some cases, they provide an opportunity for voters to endorse or reject something their state legislature wants to do. In others, regular citizens can get their preferred policy on the ballot directly through a signature-gathering campaign.

Here's a rundown of the results of some of the major measures on statewide ballots this year.

The Supreme Court's 2022 decision to overturn the nationwide abortion protections established by Roe v. Wade instantly turned abortion access into a state-by-state issue. It also led to a flurry of ballot measures across the country in which voters were asked to decide whether their states should protect or restrict abortion rights. In the years since, voters have generally come down in favor of protecting abortion rights.

That trend got another test this year due to abortion-related measures in four states.

In Idaho, voters rejected a measure that would have overturned their state's strict abortion restrictions and established a right to reproductive freedom and privacy, including abortion until fetal viability. The initiative's failure means Idaho will not join the ranks of red states where voters used ballot measures to expand abortion rights.

One of those red states is Missouri , where voters approved a measure in 2024 that struck down some of the nation's most restrictive abortion laws. On Tuesday, voters rejected a Republican-backed measure that would have repealed that 2024 amendment and allowed strict abortion restrictions to be put back into place. That same failed measure would also have created new limits on gender-affirming care in the state.

Voters in two other states that already have relatively permissive laws around abortion access — Nevada and Virginia — approved measures that will enshrine abortion rights in their state constitutions, a step that will make it much harder to restrict access in the future.

The debate over transgender rights, particularly when it comes to minors, has become a central issue in American politics. It should be no surprise, then, that a number of states had measures related to the topic on the ballot this year. All of them would impose new limits on transgender rights.

Four states — Washington, Nebraska, Arizona and Colorado — voted on measures that would ban trans athletes from participating on sports teams that match their gender identity.

There are some important differences from state to state, though. The proposals in Washington and Nebraska would only apply to girls' and women's teams. Colorado's and Arizona's would apply to both male and female teams.

Washington's bill also includes a stipulation that would require all K-12 students who want to play girls' or women's sports — whether they identify as trans or not — to have their sex verified by a doctor . Arizona's measure will also ban schools from allowing trans minors or adults to access bathrooms, locker rooms or other private spaces designated for a sex that doesn't match the one they were assigned at birth.

A separate initiative in Colorado would ban gender-affirming surgeries for minors.

The initiatives in Arizona and Nebraska were both approved. Washington's measure and the two initiatives in Colorado appeared to be on the path to passing as well.

The only state where potential new restrictions on transgender rights failed was Missouri, where the new limits were combined with a proposal to repeal abortion rights in the state.

Six states voted on measures related to voter ID.

California and Colorado rejected proposals that would have established or expanded requirements for voters to show ID when they cast their ballots or when voting by mail. A similar measure in Nevada was approved.

Arizona, Ohio and North Carolina, where strict voter ID requirements are already in place under state law, considered measures that add or expand those requirements in their state constitutions. Arizona's failed . The measures in Ohio and North Carolina were approved

Schools have been a major flashpoint for culture war battles in recent years. A handful of measures on the ballot Tuesday asked voters to weigh in on some of those debates.

Voters in Arizona and Wisconsin both considered proposals to ban affirmative action in schools and all other government agencies. Arizona's measure failed . Wisconsin's was approved .

Alabama voters approved a pair of school proposals. One will require public schools to play the national anthem at least once a week. The other will make the recitation of the Pledge of Allegiance a daily requirement and mandate that school boards adopt policies to allow student-led prayer.

It's still too early to know the fate of a sweeping parental rights initiative in Washington that would give parents of public school students substantially more oversight over the education their children receive, including the power to review curricula and textbooks, put strict new limits on the kinds of medical care schools can provide without parental notification and roll back changes to the state's parental rights law that protected against discrimination and bullying in schools.

Ballot measures frequently center on contentious political issues, but in recent years, the initiative process itself has increasingly become the subject of political debate.

Five states voted on measures that would have made it harder for citizen-led ballot initiatives to become law, either by raising the share of the vote certain measures need to get approved or restricting the subjects that initiatives can address. Four of those measures failed. The fifth appears to be on track to also being rejected.

Voters in North Dakota and South Dakota shot down measures that would have required any attempt to change their state constitutions to get 60% of the vote. A similar proposal in Utah that would have applied only to tax-related initiatives also failed. A California measure that would also raise the threshold for certain tax-related initiatives was trailing with more than half of the vote counted as of Wednesday afternoon.

Changing the threshold for success by 10 percentage points may not sound like a huge deal, but it is often the difference between a proposal becoming law and being rejected. For example, initiatives in Florida that would have legalized abortion and recreational marijuana use both received majority support from voters in 2024, but neither became law because they fell short of the state's 60% approval standard.

Idaho also rejected a measure that would have banned initiatives aimed at legalizing marijuana, psychedelics and other narcotics.

Two states voted to protect the initiative process, as well. Montana voters approved a proposal to amend the state's constitution to guarantee citizens' rights to pursue ballot initiatives and make it harder for the government to interfere with measures approved by voters.

In Missouri , voters approved a measure that will prohibit the state's Republican-led legislature from weakening the initiative process. It will also bar it from amending or repealing any measures that have passed unless 80% of both chambers agree to put the change before voters.

Voters across the country also weighed in on a long list of other pivotal ballot measures that don't fit neatly into a specific category. Here are a few of them.

Arizona voted to ban new traffic cameras without direct voter approval. Nebraska rejected a proposal to legalize online sports betting . Vermont voters overwhelmingly approved a measure to ban discrimination based on gender identity. Virginia voted to restore the voting rights of people convicted of felonies once they're released from prison. A measure in Wisconsin aimed at prohibiting the government from closing places of worship during public health emergencies was rejected. Massachusetts voters chose not to make recreational marijuana sales illegal.

Lower-stakes — but still noteworthy — measures included a failed Colorado initiative that would have enshrined the right to hunt and fish in the state constitution and a request for Idaho voters to select an official state gun — they chose the Winchester Model 1873 rifle.

articles.summary: Ron DeSantis warns that Tuesday's Senate losses effectively end Trump's chances of replacing Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito with conservatives.
articles.body: Republicans’ sweeping losses Tuesday could reshape the Supreme Court for years, prominent conservatives warned, arguing that Democrats’ new Senate majority may block President Donald Trump from replacing Justices Clarence Thomas or Samuel Alito with conservative successors. "Assuming Republicans lose the seats where prediction markets have the Democrats at 90+% to win, that would produce 55 Democrat Senate seats," Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis wrote on X on Tuesday night in a post that was viewed almost 4 million times. "Chance of confirming a worthy successor to Justice Thomas and/or Alito during President Trump’s term: Zero. Chance of confirming a worthy successor during a hypothetical GOP admin 2029-2033: probably zero (GOP won’t be able to recapture enough seats in 28)." Democrats took control of the Senate Tuesday night and hold 54 seats as of midday Wednesday, and DeSantis was joined on social media by several others explaining that Alito, 76, and Thomas, 78, will be almost impossible to replace with equally conservative appointees. AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI Ed Whelan, a conservative legal expert who clerked for the late Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia, wrote on X that Trump is now effectively blocked from appointing federal judges or Supreme Court justices during the final two years of his term. "If a Republican is elected president in 2028, that president will not be able to appoint any justices or judges until Republicans regain the Senate," Whelan wrote. "Given the deep hole, that might not happen until 2033. " Whelan also explained that a justice resigning during the upcoming "lame duck" session is highly unlikely and Republicans would have a hard time securing 51 votes. TRUMP CHEERS ALITO STAYING FOR ANOTHER SUPREME COURT TERM: 'ONE OF THE GREATEST OF ALL TIME' "If Sherrod Brown wins Ohio seat, he gets sworn into Senate in early December, so Senate becomes 52R-48D," Whelan wrote. "Collins and Murkowski would be unlikely to support anyone Trump would nominate. John Cornyn, Thom Tillis, and Bill Cassidy aren’t going to be eager to do Trump any favors. And there are other senators—e.g., John Curtis of Utah—who would be leery of anyone Trump would be eager to push through." Others on social media echoed similar sentiments. "In 2033, Clarence Thomas will turn 85 and Samuel Alito will turn 83," conservative author Hans Mahncke posted on X in response to DeSantis. "There is no reason to believe they won't still be going strong on the bench. But the larger point is absolutely valid. No one lives forever, and if these two great men are not eventually replaced by genuinely conservative justices, America will go the way of the rest of the Western world." articles.title: Chuck Schumer after sweeping Democratic midterm victories: 'I'll be re-elected as majority leader'
articles.summary: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer says he'll be re-elected as majority leader despite five newly elected Democratic senators opposing his bid.
articles.body:
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said late Wednesday morning that he would be selected as majority leader in the next Congress, despite opposition from some of the newly elected Democrats who will join the upper chamber come January.

During his press conference, the New York senator initially resisted questions from reporters about the inner workings of the Senate, including whether he would be open to getting rid of the filibuster.

The second time Schumer was asked about whether he'd be the one leading Senate Democrats next year, he caved and offered a more concrete response.

"OK, again, to repeat the answer, the issue is not me. I'll be re-elected as majority leader. But the issue is focusing on the American people and what they want," Schumer said.

To become majority leader, Schumer would need the support of a simple majority of the Senate Democratic caucus.

No incumbent Democratic senator has publicly said they will oppose Schumer in the closed-door leadership vote, but five newly elected senators have. They are Adam Hamilton of Kansas; Julia Stratton of Illinois; Troy Jackson of Maine; Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota; and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.

James Talarico of Texas has not said whether he would support Schumer, largely steering clear of the party's internal leadership debate ahead of his election victory.

Five confirmed votes against Schumer won't be enough to tank his chances, and no one else has sought to challenge him for the leadership post.

At Wednesday's press event, Schumer wanted the focus to be on the Democrats — their overwhelming win and what they plan to do with it.

He described what happened last night as "a generational remake of the Senate map that is going to change America not only now, but on into the future."

"Many of the folks who voted for us yesterday, of course, are still skeptical. That's OK. These voters did not give us the majority so we can do whatever we want," Schumer added. "They entrusted us with the majority to do what they, the American people, want. Republicans received that opportunity two years ago and completely squandered it."

Schumer's read of Americans' mood is that they want the cost of living to be eased and government corruption to be dealt with.

Ending the Iran war, one of the main drivers of stubbornly elevated energy prices , was another priority the Democrats will pursue, Schumer said.

He also claimed that Republicans believed President Donald Trump's victory in 2024 gave them a "mandate to do Trump's self-serving bidding."

Regarding Trump, Schumer said the Senate will launch investigations into him whenever he "defies the will of the American people or the law."

"Elections have always been the strongest lever Americans have to counter a wannabe king, so long as Americans are willing to use it. Yesterday, America did," Schumer said. "Americans have never lost faith that they can change this country with their vote. The onus is now on us to prove them right."

articles.title: Trump 'couldn't transfer the love' of his supporters to other Republicans amid historic midterm loss
articles.summary: Donald Trump said he "couldn't transfer the love" from his rally supporters to Republican candidates after Democrats swept the midterm elections.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump said he "couldn't transfer the love" his supporters hold for him to other Republican candidates in his first public appearance after Democrats captured the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate in Tuesday's midterm elections.

"If I were on the ballot, we would have won. You saw the people that were packed. Thousands and thousands of people at every rally. And if I was on the ballot, we would have won," he said while taking questions at a ceremony to raise the final steel beam for the ballroom Wednesday.

"But they just... You couldn't transfer that love. There was such love at those rallies. It was incredible. And, we weren't able to transfer the love to candidates," he said.

Trump did not address the election loss during his initial remarks, choosing to focus solely on the ballroom's construction until he took questions from reporters.

Trump did address the election after being asked if he agreed with Vice President JD Vance's assessment that the Iran war cost Republicans the election.

"I think it's largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term and probably that's, probably it's true," he admitted.

"But at the same time, if I had it to do again, I'd have to do it again, because long term, it's the only answer. You can't let Iran have a nuclear war," Trump added.

The president also said he felt the tradeoff was worth it.

"You have no choice. I mean, I thought the oil would go up a lot more, and I did it on that basis. You have no choice. You have to do it. You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon or everything that you see here someday might not exist," he said.

Trump then addressed criticisms of his Monday speech in front of the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool after being asked if he regretted the speech's timing.

"I heard it was a very good speech, got great reviews. That was only a speech on the reflecting pool that had nothing to do with anything else. That was a speech, very much like this is today on this incredible place that we're building at the White House. It's going to be here for many, many years and serving our country," he said.

He also reflected on a lengthy post-mortem social media post from Vance that pinned Republicans' Tuesday losses largely on the Iran war. In the post, Vance cited four primary things Republicans can do to win back voters : "1) End the war 2) Focus on cost of living/inflation 3) Put America First 4) Change our relationship to Israel."

Trump was asked if he had any idea Vance was going to publish the remarks.

"I know how he feels about it. I think it was, I think it was fine. Yeah, I thought it was good. We knew that, I know that. I knew that when I went in and we stopped them from having a nuclear weapon. And they will never have a nuclear weapon," he said.

Despite Democrats' capture of large majorities in both the House and Senate, Trump appeared hopeful that he could still work with them.

"I'll get along probably with the Democrats, unless they want to be destructive. But I have the power of the veto. So if we don't like what they're doing or they'll... they've already called and they want to talk about things and that's fine," he remarked.

He also downplayed the likelihood that Democrats would move to impeach him or members of his Cabinet.

"I think it would. I think it would destroy... I think it would destroy the Democrat Party if they did it. Because impeachment for no reason. What? For having a successful country? Our country is more successful now than in any time in its history," he told a reporter before saying, "Watch the beam go up."

articles.title: NYC's Mamdani says Abdul El-Sayed's Senate victory in Michigan 'means so much to so many'
articles.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani praised Abdul El-Sayed's Michigan Senate win over Republican Mike Rogers, describing it as "incredibly exciting."
articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Wednesday that Abdul El-Sayed's Senate election victory in Michigan "is one that means so much to so many." El-Sayed, who will become the first Muslim U.S. senator in history, toppled former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers in what was one of the most-watched contests of the election. "I haven't spoken to him yet. I'm sure he is quite busy. I've had the privilege of speaking to him in the past, and I have to say that his election is one that means so much to so many," Mamdani said Wednesday. "And to see to see that victory in the face that all that he had to reckon with over the course of that campaign, whether in terms of the extraordinary amount of money spent to oppose him or the racism and slander that he was met with on a daily basis, it is incredibly exciting to see as he said last night, that the good guys won," Mamdani added. ABDUL EL-SAYED DELIVERS MAJOR BLOW TO GOP IN MICHIGAN AFTER BRUISING SENATE RACE Mamdani added that "what last night showed us is that Americans are tired of being told that their needs are unrealistic by politicians who have been bought by the wealthiest people in the country. "This country has elected a new generation of leadership, a generation with a mandate to lower the cost of living, to build, not bomb, to never betray the working people who entrusted them with power," he added. "And I hear often that the politics that we're fighting for here in New York City are not possible outside of city limits. And what last night showed us is that working people are the majority, whether we are speaking of Austin or Ann Arbor or Astoria, and it is time to put those same people first in our politics and last night shows us that it's possible to do so all across the country." STATE OF PLAY: BLUE WAVE SWEEPS DEMOCRATS INTO POWER, WITH KEY RACES STILL HANGING IN BALANCE Democrats regained control of the House and Senate during Tuesday's midterm elections, but Mamdani said that "it is not enough for us as Democrats to win power. articles.title: Trump touts White House ballroom as Democrats celebrate midterm blue wave
articles.summary: One day after Democrats delivered a decisive midterm victory, Trump visited the site of the White House ballroom to tout its construction.
articles.body:
WASHINGTON − President Donald Trump 's first public appearance after Republicans' midterm shellacking? An activity he said relaxes him. He returned to his White House ballroom site and gave a detailed update on its construction.

He visited the site on Nov. 4 to watch the installation of the controversial project's final beam and speak to construction workers. Drone proof, missile proof, bullet proof − it will be the "safest place" in Washington, when it opens, Trump said in an impromptu speech.

"I doubt there's a ballroom in the country with 50-foot ceilings," Trump said. "There's never been anything built like this, and it's for the country, and it's free. When it's completed, it'll be the best anywhere in the world."

He pushed back on critics who have targeted his DC renovation and beatifications projects.

"I'm doing it because the White House is the ultimate symbol of America," Trump said, though he also acknowledged his love for construction projects. "For me, it's relaxing. For somebody else, it's the opposite."

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum called it a "day of celebration" and referred to Trump as the "greatest builder" who has ever been president.

The event largely mirrored the president's final pitch to voters ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, when he spoke at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool to tout his Washington construction projects. The president spoke then for 20 minutes before bringing up the looming midterms.

The following day, Democrats won control of the House and Senate in a seismic blue wave that saw them push deep into red territory. Trump had urged Republicans to "pretend I'm on the ballot," but Democrats flipped seven Senate seats including in South Carolina, Kansas and Texas.

In the final stretch of the campaign, Trump, who has a record-low approval rating, crisscrossed the country to hold more than two dozen rallies for Republicans. In doing so, he turned the election into a referendum on his presidency.

Still, Trump said on Nov. 4 he had no regrets. He told USA TODAY that if he were on the ballot, Republicans would have won.

"You saw the people. They were packed. Thousands and thousands of people at every rally," Trump said. "There was such love at those rallies, it was incredible. We weren't able to transfer the love to candidates."

Trump admitted in the immediate aftermath of the election that the Iran war contributed to the defeat, which Vice President JD Vance also said following the GOP's losses.

"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so," Vance said in a social media post. "Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest."

Addressing reporters later in the afternoon, Trump said Vance's assessment was "largely true," but he believed the military conflict was worth it in the end.

"At the same time, if I had to do it again, I'd have to do it again," Trump said.

After another round of questions, he asked press if they wanted to see his helipad. "Should I walk out the other way?" Trump said to an aide as reporters looked out onto the South Lawn.

He walked out through his ballroom, to a round of applause from construction workers.

articles.title: Conservative US Supreme Court justices Thomas and Alito in spotlight after Democratic landslide
articles.summary: By John Kruzel WASHINGTON, Nov 4 (Reuters) - The US midterm election landslide that gives Democrats control of Congress starting in January is fueling questi...
articles.body:
Swearing-in ceremony for incoming Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh

WASHINGTON, Nov 4 (Reuters) - The US midterm election landslide that gives Democrats control of Congress starting in January is fueling questions about the longevity of the Supreme Court's two eldest justices, Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito, and the durability of its conservative majority.

As Republicans prepare to cede control of the Senate to Democrats for the next two years or ‌more, some conservative commentators already are expressing concerns about the health prospects of Thomas, 78, and Alito, 76, placing renewed focus on their continued service on the top US judicial body.

The US Constitution ‌assigns the Senate the power to confirm a president's judicial nominations. With a Senate majority, Democrats can block any nominations that Republican President Donald Trump would make to fill potential Supreme Court vacancies, just as Republicans blocked Democratic President Barack Obama from filling one in ​2016.

Thomas has given no public indication of wanting to step down. Alito said last month he would remain for the duration of the current nine-month term, which began in October, even if Democrats were to retake the Senate. Thomas and Alito did not immediately respond to questions from Reuters about whether they are considering retiring.

Thomas and Alito are the court's two most conservative justices and have reliably backed Trump policies in major rulings during his second term in office. The court's 6-3 conservative majority, which has steered American law in a sharply rightward direction on issues from abortion to gun rights to presidential powers, includes three justices Trump appointed during his first term as president.

Alito's comment about remaining ‌through the current term followed speculation that he might quickly retire in the ⁠event Democrats captured the Senate in order to ensure that Trump could get a successor confirmed with Republicans still in control.

Until Democrats formally take over Congress on January 3, the current Republican majority retains control during what is called a lame-duck session.

While some conservatives might want Thomas or Alito to retire right away so Trump can nominate a ⁠replacement and a Republican-led Senate could quickly provide confirmation, the tight timeline and other legislative priorities could make that difficult even if the justices had any interest in doing so.

To some legal analysts, the notion of an imminent Supreme Court departure seemed far-fetched.

Although justices mulling retirement often consider the politics of the president and party control of the Senate in making a decision, "they do not like to broadcast that they do so," Cornell Law School professor Michael Dorf said.

"Absent an acute ​health ​crisis," Dorf said, "a decision to retire in the next several months would appear, and would in fact be, so nakedly political ​that I doubt Justice Alito or Thomas would take it."

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, a ‌prominent Republican who mounted an unsuccessful presidential campaign in 2024, wrote on social media: "Chance of confirming a worthy successor to Justice Thomas and/or Alito during President Trump's term: Zero."

The size of the new Democratic majority in the Senate could make it difficult for Republicans to reclaim the chamber in the 2028 elections, according to some analysts, meaning Republicans may not control both the presidency and Senate for quite some time.

"If a Republican is elected president in 2028, that president will not be able to appoint any justices or judges until Republicans regain the Senate," said legal analyst Ed Whelan of the Ethics and Public Policy Center, who served as a Justice Department official under Republican President George W. Bush.

"Given the deep hole, that might not happen until 2033," Whelan said.

Thomas would be 84 and Alito 82 in 2033 when a new Congress is sworn in. That would place them over ‌the average retirement age of around 80 for Supreme Court justices since 2000.

Thomas and Alito have no serious health ​concerns that are publicly known, though each was briefly hospitalized in recent years. Alito was treated for dehydration in March after feeling ​ill during an event in Philadelphia. Thomas missed arguments in cases in 2022 when he was hospitalized ​with flu-like symptoms.

Three justices have died in office this century. Conservative Chief Justice William Rehnquist died in 2005 at age 80. Conservative Justice Antonin Scalia died in 2016 at ‌79. Liberal Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg died in 2020 at 87.

A Republican-led Senate refused ​to consider Obama's nominee to replace Scalia, allowing Trump the ​following year to fill the vacancy.

The Senate confirmed Trump's nominee Amy Coney Barrett swiftly in the weeks after Ginsburg's death to build the court's current 6-3 conservative edge. Ginsburg's decision not to retire during Obama's presidency to clear the way for a like-minded successor was seen by many liberals as a serious miscalculation that led to a dramatically more conservative court.

Some conservative legal commentators addressed the possible ​political and actuarial implications if Democrats keep the Senate for years.

"The Senate is ‌lost until 2032, so I hope Thomas and Alito got on their treadmills this morning," Ilya Shapiro, a senior fellow and director of constitutional studies at the Manhattan Institute, wrote in a ​social media post.

Josh Hammer, a Newsweek podcaster and former clerk to Judge James Ho of the New Orleans-based 5th US Circuit Court of Appeals, wrote in a social media post: "I ​hope Clarence Thomas and Sam Alito have historically great health insurance plans."

(Reporting by John Kruzel; Editing by Will Dunham)

articles.summary: (The Center Square)—The outcome of a tightly contested and controversial U. S.
articles.body:
(The Center Square)—The outcome of a tightly contested and controversial U.S. Senate race in Alaska may not be known until the end of the month or later.

U.S. Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, a Republican, is making a bid for a third six-year term. As of 2:20 p.m. EDT, he trails former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola, a Democrat, by 626 votes with 77% of ballots counted. He has 102,075 votes to her 102,701. The race has been the focus of controversy after The New York Times reported that Peltola's campaign helped recruit a candidate with the same name as Sullivan in an apparent attempt to confuse voters. She has denied doing that.

Twenty-three percent of votes have yet to be tallied. Even when they are, the narrow margin separating the candidates means that the outcome may be decided not at the state's polling sites but through the mail via absentee and questioned ballots.

In the previous midterm congressional election four years ago, Alaska officials said they received 9,143 in-person absentee ballots and 8,009 questioned ballots. Two years ago, in the presidential election, state officials reported receiving 18,158 in-person absentee ballots and 15,138 questioned ballots. Voters can ask for a mail-in ballot and still vote in person, so the number of outstanding votes in the state's general elections in 2022 and 2024 is unclear.

Steve Kirch, public relations manager for the state's division of elections, did not immediately return an interview request.

What is clear is the 49th s tate's deadline for counting all votes.

By Nov. 13, absentee ballots from the 50 states plus its territories as well as Puerto Rico, Guam, the Virgin Islands, and American Samoa should have arrived and must be postmarked by Nov. 3. By Nov. 18, all ballots from overseas addresses must be received and postmarked by Election Day. By Nov. 19, the State Review Board begins its review of election materials, and by Nov. 25, state officials expect to certify the election results.

In addition, Alaska has ranked choice voting. Peltola or Sullivan will need to receive more than 50 percent of the first-choice votes after officials have counted them all. If neither does, the last-place candidate is eliminated. Then, state officials redistribute that candidate's ballots according to voters' second and subsequent choices. The process continues until a candidate receives a majority, or 50% plus one vote.

Despite the state's deadlines, federal officials may complicate them.

The Justice Department has sent a target letter to prominent Democratic elections attorney Marc Elias asking about his possible involvement in petitioning a retired teacher by the name of Dan J. Sullivan to run for Alaska's Senate seat, according to the Associated Press.

An email to the Justice Department's press office requesting comment was not immediately returned.

articles.title: The biggest winners and losers of the 2026 midterm elections
articles.summary: Among the winners: Black political power, Jon Ossoff and Ron DeSantis. Among the losers: Donald Trump, Elon Musk and really ugly campaign tactics.
articles.body:
The results are still rolling in on the 2026 midterm elections. But the overall contours of what just happened are already obvious: A historic Democratic victory, and a historic setback for what is now the lame-duck presidency of Donald Trump.

A look at some of the big winners and losers that tell the tale.

Black political power : Before Tuesday, only three Black governors had ever been elected. Next year, we'll have five serving at the same time . That's after wins by Florida GOP Gov.-elect Byron Donalds, Wisconsin Democratic Gov.-elect David Crowley, Nevada Democratic Gov.-elect Aaron Ford and Georgia Democratic Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms, who will be the first Black female governor ever. Also, Democrats won in the South due in large part to a surge of Black voters. And if a Black Democrat — Scott Colom — can beat Mississippi GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a Trump +23 state with its fair share of history with race issues, it will be perhaps the biggest statement of all.

The religious left : Two of the biggest Democratic over-performers Tuesday were Kansas Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton, who is a pastor, and Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico, who basically sounds like a youth pastor and often cited his faith on the trail. Bet on Democrats looking for more candidates like them, starting today.

Jon Ossoff, times two : He won reelection to the Senate by a stunning 18-point margin in a swing state, bolstering his fast-rising national star. And Lance Bottoms' win means he can run for president in 2028 without worrying about a major obstacle: a governor who would replace him with a Republican.

James Talarico : He had a deeply flawed opponent in Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, yes. But virtually nobody had him winning by double-digits. (He's currently ahead by 12, in a state Democrats where the party hadn't won in a statewide race since 1994.)

Gina Hinojosa : But don't sleep on the other big statewide Democratic winner in Texas, Gov.-elect Hinojosa. She appealed to voters of all walks from all corners of the state, and she beat a three-term GOP governor in Greg Abbott who was on nobody's radar at the start of the election.

Annie Andrews : Also expect plenty of focus on the South Carolina senator-elect. The pediatrician benefitted from appointed GOP Sen. Darline Graham's problems, but Andrews was well-liked in her own right in preelection polling. She ran a very strong campaign.

Democrats' presidential hopes : Not only do Ossoff, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro and other potential 2028 hopefuls emerge smelling like roses, but Democrats proved they can compete all over the place . If they can make Texas competitive — a big if , sure — it completely recasts the Electoral College math in their favor. And Tuesday's results suggest the Trump coalition, which we already knew didn't turn up as much when he's not on the ballot, is crumbling.

Democrats' power in the state : We're still awaiting some key results, but Democrats have gained full control of at least six state governments , per Bolts magazine's Daniel Nichanian. The GOP has long benefitted from superior control in the states.

The Supreme Court's left flank : The size of Democrats' Senate majority makes the GOP's ability to confirm a conservative justice to replace Samuel Alito and/or Clarence Thomas appear rather distant — possibly as distant as the early 2030s, Florida GOP Gov. Ron DeSantis argued late Tuesday .

Ron DeSantis : OK, it's not just him. But Tuesday was an argument for the GOP to look outside the Trump administration — and beyond Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio — for their 2028 nominee. Florida was at least one of the few states were Republicans notched some key wins, and DeSantis has created some distance from Trump's political approach of late. Also keep an eye on outgoing Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp, who is even less tethered to Trumpism. ( Vance's X post Wednesday blaming the Iran war for GOP losses suggests he sees the need to distance himself, too.)

Washington, DC, lawyers : The Trump administration's laissez-faire approach to ethics and self-enrichment has given Democrats a bevy of potential targets. Incoming Democratic House Oversight Committee Chairman Rep. Robert Garcia of California said it all late Tuesday in a two-word statement: "Lawyer up." (And administration figures already had been .)

Donald Trump : It's obvious, but it's hard to overstate what a rebuke this election was to the president personally. Not only did Trump suffer a crippling loss that leaves him as a lame duck; he made the GOP campaign overwhelmingly about him. He took sole ownership of the economy with his tariffs and the Iran war in ways that clearly backfired. He meddled in GOP primaries in ways that produced a slate of less-electable candidates (a repeat of 2018 that suggests he didn't learn any lessons there). And his conduct down the stretch in the campaign was downright bizarre, dismissing affordability concerns and frequently focusing on overwhelmingly unpopular things like the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool less than 24 hours before Election Day. There are no good signs about what lay ahead for the GOP and Trump over the next two years, but Republicans are still clearly afraid to blame him.

JD Vance : Trump is now the millstone around his neck. He can try to distance himself from Trump on the Iran war and Israel — as he clearly set about trying to do on Wednesday — but it's going to be an exceedingly difficult thing to do. Trump, after all, won't want his VP constantly undercutting his policies and supposed legacy items like the Iran war. And Trump isn't one who willingly takes the heat to help other members of his party.

Elon Musk : He spent hundreds of millions of dollars on the GOP — including much of it specifically on one of the party's biggest flops, the Texas Senate race. Indeed, much like in the 2025 Wisconsin Supreme Court race, it seemed to give Democrats a bogeyman to run against — their own Republican version of George Soros. Also, he moved Tesla to Texas in recent years, and now it's governed by Democrats.

The tariffs : This was Trump's and the GOP's original sin. Voters seemed open to the idea, but it's not clear they really knew what tariffs were. Then Trump implemented them in bizarre, scattershot and on-again-off-again fashion. A recent study from the New York Federal Reserve found that the overall cost of consumer goods would have fallen without his tariffs in 2025. Congressional Republicans must be ruing that they didn't assert their authority — or at least try harder to talk Trump out of it.

Mike Johnson : The GOP House speaker claimed for weeks that the polls were wrong and — rather laughably — that Republicans were going to "defy history" by keeping their House majority. He was either just saying stuff, or he has terrible political intel. And now he's not even going to try to stay in charge of the House GOP; he won't run for House minority leader (though maybe he's looking forward to giving up one of the most thankless jobs in Washington).

GOP poll denialists : But Johnson wasn't the only one; a whole bunch of Republicans confidently predicted that the polls were under-sampling Trump's supporters. In the end, the polls actually under-estimated Democrats — and often by some significant margins.

The GOP's gerrymanders : Not only did the GOP's map in North Carolina majorly blow up in its face (they're either on track to lose or are trailing in 10 out of 14 seats), but the party might fail to win any of the five seats it drew for itself in Texas and the four it drew for itself in Florida. It looks like the GOP's whole brazen mid-decade redistricting push gained it next to nothing, at least in this election. And Democrats newfound control in many states means they could redraw their own maps ahead of the 2028 election, thanks to the precedent the GOP has now set.

Previous wave elections : Sorry, 2010 and 2006. Apologies, 1994. The 2026 election appears to have set the post-Watergate benchmark for a political rout in a midterm election. Democrats appear to have won the popular vote by around 13 points, which would be the largest margin for any party since 1976 , per the Economist.

Darline Graham : It almost seems cruel to put her here, because she never seemed to truly ask for any of this after her brother died. And you could certainly blame Trump for the weird decision to elevate her. But the appointed senator turned out to be a disastrous candidate, with voters overwhelmingly saying she didn't have the qualifications to be a senator. It's a cautionary tale for anyone who might feel compelled to throw themselves into the cauldron of national politics.

Roger Marshall : It can feel difficult to isolate the truly bad candidates when voters were generally so against the GOP. But Marshall is certainly near the top of that list. His fundraising was anemic and he didn't seem to really have much of a campaign operation until it was too late. He also reportedly went rogue late in the campaign by cutting a video explaining his pursuit of his medical patients' debts. In the end, he lost a Trump +16 state by around 5 points.

Ken Paxton : Paxton's under-performance was even bigger. He is losing a Trump + 14 state by 12 points — a massive 26-point swing.

Haley Stevens : The Democratic Michigan congresswoman's late decision to flip her endorsement from her former primary opponent Abdul El-Sayed to Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers in the Michigan Senate race doesn't seem to have made any difference, judging by El-Sayed's seven-point win. About all it appears to have done is doom any shot Stevens had at a career in Democratic politics.

Really ugly campaign tactics : Vivek Ramaswamy's ugly and controversial ad featuring Democrat Amy Acton's mom didn't work; he did worse than any other statewide Ohio Republican. The GOP's transgender slurs about Andrews and efforts to suggest James Talarico was a gay vegan seemed to do basically no good, as those two were among Democrats' biggest over-performers. The situation is a little less clear in Alaska, where Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola might still win after the New York Times reported that her campaign recruited a decoy Dan Sullivan; counting those votes will still take some time. Politics has plenty of ugly campaign tactics, but maybe voters don't like ones that are so transparent and desperate? At the very least, these gambits didn't seem to help.

Democrats stepping aside for independents : Independent Dan Osborn's six-point loss to Nebraska GOP Sen. Pete Ricketts suggests Democrats didn't glean much from their strategy of trying to let independents run with no Democratic opponents in dark-red states. Independents also lost by more than 20 points in similar set-ups in Idaho and South Dakota. And in Montana, their failure to get the Democratic nominee to drop out meant she and the independent split about half the vote. Tuesday's results suggest Democrats might as well run moderate Democrats who fit those states.

articles.title: Newsom solicits cash as Biden’s former election lawyer mobilizes legal team for Mississippi Senate race
articles.summary: Gavin Newsom is soliciting emergency donations while Marc Elias' law firm prepares for a legal fight as the Mississippi Senate race remains uncalled.
articles.body:
Democratic heavyweights Gavin Newsom and Marc Elias are mobilizing behind Scott Colom as the Mississippi Senate race remains too close to call, with the California governor soliciting emergency donations and Elias' law firm preparing for a legal fight over the final count.

In an overnight fundraising email obtained by Fox News Digital, Newsom's campaign told supporters, "Please help asap," warning that the race was entering "a phase of ballot curing and possible legal fights." Elias said his firm is "leading the legal effort to ensure" Colom wins.

"As you read this, Scott leads the Republican incumbent by just a couple hundred votes," the email said. "There is no way Republicans are giving up this Senate seat without a fight. The job is not finished!"

The Mississippi Senate race between Colom and incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, R-Miss., remained uncalled Wednesday because thousands of ballots had yet to be processed. Colom led Hyde-Smith by just 43 votes in incomplete, unofficial results, while an estimated 44,000 ballots remained outstanding, including absentee, affidavit and provisional ballots.

"Scott Colom is going to be the next Senator from Mississippi. I am proud that Elias Law Group is leading the legal effort to ensure that happens," Elias wrote on his Bluesky account.

Elias is a longtime Democratic election lawyer who served as general counsel to Hillary Clinton's 2016 presidential campaign and led a Perkins Coie legal team representing Joe Biden's 2020 campaign.

He later founded Elias Law Group, which has represented Democratic campaign committees and candidates in high-profile election disputes.

Fox News Digital reached out to Elias for additional details about his planned involvement in Mississippi's U.S. Senate race but did not receive a response in time for publication.

Mississippi law allows absentee ballots postmarked by Election Day to arrive within five business days — through Nov. 10 — and permits voters to cure certain ballot problems during that period.

The Mississippi Democratic Party has also filed a court challenge alleging delayed polling-place openings, long lines and ballot shortages in DeSoto County.

articles.title: Hakeem Jeffries declares bid for House speaker after GOP's midterm massacre
articles.summary: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is officially running to be Speaker of the House after Republicans' midterm losses on Tuesday night.
articles.body:
Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., is officially running to be Speaker of the House in the next Congress.

It comes after Democrats made historic gains in Tuesday night's midterm elections, taking back both the House and Senate for the remainder of President Donald Trump's term.

Jeffries sent a letter to fellow House Democrats on Wednesday afternoon congratulating them on their victories and adding, "I write to humbly request your support in connection with my candidacy to serve as the next Speaker of the House of Representatives."

Jeffries told reporters that he intended to run for the top job in the House during a press conference with his top deputies on Wednesday, House Minority Whip Katherine Clark, D-Mass., and House Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif.

Clark and Aguilar also signaled they would run for the No. 2 and No. 3 positions in the House.

And despite a small group of far-left socialists elected to Congress who are expected to pose a headache for Jeffries and other establishment Democrats, he will likely have little trouble winning the speaker's gavel given the wide majority his party won on Tuesday.

At the time of writing this story, Democrats were projected to win 237 seats compared to 139 for the GOP.

But 59 races are still too close to call, and Jeffries told reporters earlier that he anticipated a total of 255 or more Democrats in the House next year.

In his lengthy letter to colleagues on Wednesday, Jeffries touted past victories and outlined his vision for the next two years.

He pledged to "try to find bipartisan common ground whenever and wherever possible" on the issue of affordability while also criticizing the right's handling of high cost-of-living.

"Donald Trump and House Republicans promised to lower costs on Day One. They failed. Instead, toxic GOP policies like the Trump tariffs and war in Iran have done the exact opposite," he wrote.

Jeffries also vowed "accountability" for the Trump administration, writing the House "will assume its place as a check and balance on an out-of-control executive branch."

He suggested Democrats would seek to undo Republicans' Medicaid cuts, extend enhanced Obamacare tax credits that expired at the beginning of this year, and end Trump's war in Iran.

"Finally, we must restore classic American values like liberty and justice for all, equal protection under the law, the unfettered right to vote in a representative democracy and our heritage as a nation of immigrants. To that end, I look forward to drawing upon the insights and perspectives of every single part of the Caucus in the days and weeks ahead. House Democrats must deliver dramatic change," Jeffries wrote.

House Democrats are slated to hold their leadership elections in mid-December.

Meanwhile on the right, House Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, and House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., will be vying for the role of minority leader in the next Congress.
