articles.title: Newsom breaks with socialists over billionaire tax, and California voters appear poised to reject it
articles.summary: California's Prop 40 billionaire tax pits the Democratic Socialists of America against Gavin Newsom, who backs a countermeasure to block it.
articles.body: In the lead-up to the November midterms, the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) put its support behind California’s Proposition 40, a measure that would impose a one-time 5% tax on billionaires in the state. Although the secretary of state's election results show it on the path to defeat as of Wednesday afternoon, the DSA’s support for the policy has created a flashpoint for larger discussions about socialism's redistributive aims and the capital flight critics say could follow. "In their mind, every tax they do is some attempt to get money from people who create wealth and move it to the state," Richard Stern, an economics scholar with Advancing American Freedom (AAF), said in an interview with Fox News Digital. The DSA's stance on Proposition 40 has also brought it into conflict with other Democratic figures, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, who opposed it. SHOCKING PERCENTAGE OF DEMOCRATS IDENTIFY AS 'DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS' ACCORDING TO NEW POLL: 'TOXIC POLICIES' The proposition would have applied a 5% tax on assets like businesses, securities, art, collectibles and intellectual property while excluding select pensions, real estate and retirement accounts. To prevent billionaires from simply leaving the state, Proposition 40 was designed to retroactively apply to billionaires who were residents of California on Jan. 1, 2026. On the website for its California chapter, the group offered a PowerPoint slideshow supporters could use to argue its merits. "We have the money in California to pay for the quality schools and healthcare that we need. It just needs to be transferred from the wrong pockets to the right ones. We can do that by taxing the rich," the slideshow reads. The DSA argued the policy would help cover up to a projected $100 billion shortfall in federal funding for the state’s Medi-Cal program that provides health insurance for low-income individuals, seniors and people with disabilities. The proposition also outlined that 90% of the generated revenue would go to healthcare, while the remaining 10% would be set aside for education, food assistance and administration of the tax. As part of its argument in favor of the policy, the DSA framed it as a scaled-up version of something that already exists: a progressive tax, a kind of tax that scales relative to income. "It calls for a temporary 5% wealth tax on just 250 Californians — the very richest people in the state — who together own $2 trillion in wealth," its materials explain. "Let’s be clear: if the Billionaire Tax passes, none of the billionaires will actually lose money. They have been averaging a growth rate of 7 or 8 percent per year in their wealth. Thus, a 5% hit doesn’t even cut into what they have; it just slightly slows down the growth of that wealth." But to experts like Stern, the AAF economist, the policy reflects a fundamental misunderstanding of wealth. "The left looks at a billionaire, and they assume that they’re sitting on $10 billion, $100 billion in cash. I hate to break it to them: There’s no cash," Stern said. "They have no idea that we’re talking about a trillion-dollar company, we’re talking about a trillion dollars’ worth of factories and warehouses and delivery trucks and machinery." LET SOCIALISTS ROB FROM THE RICH 100%, AND YOU STILL WON’T BE ABLE TO PAY THE BILLS Notably, Newsom has said he is opposed to the measure, arguing it would put California at a competitive disadvantage. In an interview with Fox News Digital, Newsom cited opposition from a number of different groups. "The firefighters opposed it. The teachers opposed it. Planned Parenthood opposed it. The vast majority of labor opposes it. I think the majority of Californians oppose it. So, we all have our reasons why," Newsom said ahead of the election. "I don’t think it’s a good idea to do [it] at a state level. It’s a badly written initiative. It focuses just on one part of the state’s budget. It’s one-time money and the impact is already being felt. People have left the state." Instead, Newsom called on voters to adopt a poison pill countermeasure. Proposition 42 was designed to prohibit new state taxes on personal property and restrict certain retroactive taxes. That measure looks to be on track to succeed. Even so, Newsom noted that his views on a 5% tax might change if implemented at the federal level. "Looking at that from a national prism, very different conversation than a state-by-state prism. That’s been the debate in California. I think the majority of Californians see that distinction even though they absolutely believe that we need a new tax bracket in this country," Newsom said. Stern noted that Newsom’s openness to considering such a policy nationally comes with many of the same difficulties, but on an international scale. 'CASTRO'S PLAYBOOK': EX-AG WARNS DOZENS OF CONGRESSIONAL BILLS ARE PUSHING SOCIALIST IDEAS "You can more easily leave California, but you could give up American citizenship and move abroad," Stern said. "[It] gets back to the old half-joke about communism and the wall in Berlin, which is, as Reagan said, they build walls that keep people in where normally we build walls to keep people out." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP When asked what distinguishes Proposition 40 from a simple tax increase, Stern pointed back to the policy’s implications for businesses, in his view, the main source of most billionaires’ wealth. "We're taking the means of production out of the hands of people that built those businesses, that manage those businesses, and giving them to Bernie Sanders and AOC and politicians to run them," Stern said, referring to two of the country’s most well-known congressional figures who have received backing from the DSA in the past. "That’s socialism."

articles.title: How Mississippi became an unlikely Senate battleground
articles.summary: An unpopular president, a charismatic Democratic candidate and an incumbent who has underperformed other Republicans in recent elections have turned a US Sen...
articles.body:
An unpopular president , a charismatic Democratic candidate and an incumbent who has underperformed other Republicans in recent elections have turned a US Senate race in Mississippi into the nail-biter of the midterms.

As of Wednesday afternoon, Democrat Scott Colom was just a few dozen votes ahead of Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a contest that remains too close to call but underscores the midterms' seismic shift toward Democrats, even in deep-red territory.

The race could come down to roughly 15,000 provisional ballots, according to Colom's campaign, still pending verification. But in the meantime, both sides expressed confidence they will prevail.

"Once the process plays out, where we are, where the ballots are, we're gonna win," Colom said during a news conference Wednesday. "And it's because the people of Mississippi turned out in historic numbers to make this race possible in a midterm election."

In a statement, Hyde-Smith campaign manager Jake Monssen said the team is "closely monitoring" the thousands of ballots still outstanding in the race.

"We remain confident that when every legally cast vote is fully and accurately counted, Mississippians will have reelected Cindy Hyde-Smith," he added.

The close race comes after Colom campaigned relentlessly to become the first Black senator from Mississippi since the Reconstruction era. The 43-year-old local district attorney argued repeatedly that the Republican headwinds and state's significant Black electorate – which at 35% is the largest of any state – would put the GOP bastion in contention with enough attention and money.

He got both, with several Democratic super PACs making last-minute ad buys and a parade of his party's biggest names, including former Vice President Kamala Harris , joining him on the stump in the campaign's waning weeks.

Groups such as the Democracy Alliance – a network of liberal donors – also made early investments to build the infrastructure to support Democrats in the state, including helping the state branch of the NAACP open 11 voter registration sites to boost Black turnout. The NAACP said it registered more than 17,000 voters this year.

Black voters made up about 30% of voters in the race, according to the CNN Voter Poll , with nearly all of them breaking for Colom.

"Mississippians showed up and shocked the nation," Derrick Johnson, the president and CEO of the NAACP, said in a statement Wednesday.

On the Republican side, President Donald Trump joined Hyde-Smith for an eleventh-hour rally to boost turnout in a state he won by 23 points just two years ago. Hyde-Smith has historically underperformed Trump after she was first appointed to the Senate 2018. In 2020, she won her first full term by 10 points, while Trump won Mississippi by 16 points that year.

During her tenure, however, Hyde-Smith also laid the groundwork for Colom's challenge when she blocked his nomination to a federal judgeship in 2023, although Colom had the backing of other Republicans, including Sen. Roger Wicker, the state's senior senator.

She objected to a donation by liberal billionaire George Soros to a PAC that backed Colom's first district attorney race. She also cited Colom's decision to sign a 2021 letter that condemned "the criminalization of transgender people and gender-affirming healthcare."

In a recent interview with CNN, Colom insisted his campaign to oust Hyde-Smith is not a grudge match. "I'm a Christian. I forgive her," he said. "Me not having a federal judgeship is not a motivating factor for me at all."

Instead, he's argued that the senator has failed her constituents in the Senate.

Colom's campaign has unleashed some of the most attention-getting ads of the midterms to argue that the incumbent had lost touch with Mississippian's economic pain. One video mocked Hyde-Smith for remarking that are "so many proteins to choose from" when asked about rising beef prices.

"Pick another protein? She done lost her damn mind. I'd rather pick another senator," one woman drawled in the ad that quickly went viral.

During the campaign, Colom deleted another ad that featured an artificial intelligence-generated depiction of Hyde-Smith running away from reporters after the state Attorney General Lynn Fitch threatened legal action against him.

Both sides now are gearing up for a legal showdown over the results as the ballot count continues.

Voter advocates and legal observers expect it could take until next week, at the earliest, for initial indications of how many of the roughly 15,000 provisional ballots – known in the state as "affidavit ballots" – will go into the final count after being vetted. Several counties in Mississippi have already started that process.

Provisional ballots are used in Mississippi for a number of reasons, such as a lack of a photo ID, a voter not being found in the pollbook — which can happen if a voter was tagged as inactive — or people submitting incomplete voter registration forms.

Voter advocates expect affidavit ballots cast by inactive voters to make up a significant share, because of a commercial credit data program the state used for the first time this cycle to clean its rolls. Those voters shouldn't need to take extra steps to see their eligibility verified, but those who were missing photo ID or had other issues will need take action to cure their ballots.

In addition to canvassing the provisional ballots, election officials will also be counting mail ballots that arrive within a five-day grace period the state allows for properly postmarked absentee ballots to be received by the elections office. That number is expected to be smaller than the affidavit ballots to be processed.

CNN's Adam Cancryn and Annie Grayer contributed to this report.

articles.title: Hegseth's future draws ominous predictions from insiders after GOP losses, but Trump isn't budging yet
articles.summary: A White House official blamed the Iran war for midterm losses and suggested Trump may hold Pete Hegseth accountable during the lame duck session.
articles.body: President Donald Trump stood by War Secretary Pete Hegseth Wednesday, saying he was doing "a very good job" even as current and former administration figures continued to question how long the Pentagon chief could remain in his post after Republicans’ bruising midterm losses. "I think he’s doing a very good job," Trump said Wednesday when asked by the media whether he was considering replacing Hegseth. The public support came a day after Democrats secured majorities in both chambers of Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections, setting the stage for a shift in power on Capitol Hill in January. The Iran war and its economic fallout loomed large in the election, with Hegseth among the administration's most vocal advocates for the campaign. His future remains the subject of speculation among current and former administration figures despite Trump's public backing. TRUMP PLEDGES TO VETO 'INSANE' DEM BILLS, PINPOINTS ISSUE PARTIALLY TO BLAME FOR REPUBLICAN LOSSES A White House official told Fox News Digital Tuesday that the election results "would have looked very different without the Iran War." The official predicted Trump would ultimately hold Hegseth, a former Fox News host, accountable, saying, "That will play out in the lame duck." "Hegseth is on the chopping block," a former White House staffer told Fox News Digital later Tuesday of Hegseth's future. An administration official said there were "signs" Hegseth could be ousted but added that "Trump can turn on a dime." The official said the possibility had been discussed for some time, though "only Trump knows what he’s gonna do." "It was clear Bessent became the go-to after Pete couldn't deliver an Iran victory," the source said, referring to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who led the sanctions campaign against Iran known as Operation Economic Outcast. Beyond the Iran war, Hegseth also championed a plan to livestream the firing-squad execution of Nidal Hasan, the former Army major who killed 13 people and wounded 32 others at Fort Hood in 2009. The proposal drew bipartisan backlash before Trump ultimately scrapped the livestream, while leaving Hasan's execution in place. A foreign policy source with ties to Hegseth expressed doubt to Fox News Digital that the secretary will remain in the job through the end of the year. The source said Republican Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie’s impeachment push could force Republicans eyeing 2028 re-election bids to "saddle themselves with a pro-Hegseth vote." GOP SEN THOM TILLIS URGES TRUMP TO REPLACE PETE HEGSETH, BLASTS PENTAGON LEADERSHIP Hegseth has faced criticism over his prominent role in the Iran war, which has continued to generate political and economic fallout long after the White House's initial three- to four-week timeline. He was among the administration's most vocal defenders of the campaign, declaring in March that the U.S. was carrying out "our retribution" against Iran. Although sustained U.S. strikes have ended, tensions with Tehran remain unresolved with lingering concerns about Iran's nuclear and missile capabilities and the possibility of renewed military action. Renewed U.S. military strikes against Iran remain under serious consideration by the White House, sources told Fox News Digital. That possibility could weigh against an immediate change at the Pentagon. Installing new leadership as the administration considers renewed military operations would create uncertainty at a critical moment, while Hegseth has already demonstrated a willingness to move quickly in carrying out Trump's military directives. Chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell told Fox News Digital Hegseth remains "100% committed to leading the Department until the end of President Trump’s term in office." "Secretary Hegseth will not back down or be deterred by politicians seeking to score partisan points or launch phony investigations where no wrongdoing exists," Parnell said. "The Department of War has followed the law, and our secretary will continue to stand and fight every single day to support and defend the Constitution, lead our troops and protect America. We will continue to drive President Trump’s agenda at the Department of War despite threats of sham witch hunts from Democrats." Democrats have signaled that Hegseth will be a focus of the incoming Congress. Before the election, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said Democrats would "run Pete Hegseth out of town" if they won the House. Democrats have also discussed investigations into the Iran war and Pentagon leadership, with impeachment among the options. Scrutiny from Democrats could keep Hegseth and the war he has championed at the center of the administration’s political troubles. Massie, R-Ky., has separately vowed to force a vote on his impeachment resolution during the lame-duck session if Hegseth remains in office. DEM FLIPS KEY SENATE SEAT IN BATTLEGROUND NORTH CAROLINA AS COOPER DEFEATS TRUMP ALLY As war secretary, Hegseth pushed sweeping changes to military culture, including banning transgender service members; eliminating diversity, equity and inclusion programs; and imposing uniform combat fitness standards for men and women. He also sought to overhaul the Pentagon bureaucracy by consolidating Army commands, cutting senior military leadership and expanding the use of artificial intelligence and advanced weapons technology. His tenure has also been marked by controversy, including the sharing of sensitive details about planned strikes against Houthi militants in Signal chats that inadvertently included a journalist. Internal infighting, leak investigations and the dismissal of several top aides have fueled scrutiny, though Trump has repeatedly defended his leadership. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The political pressure on Hegseth echoes a past moment when midterm losses and an unpopular war put a defense secretary’s future in question. On Nov. 8, 2006, President George W. Bush announced Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld’s resignation, one day after Republicans suffered major midterm election losses amid growing criticism of the Iraq War.

articles.title: Florida congressman diagnoses GOP's blue tsunami losses: 'We failed to make them think we cared about them'
articles.summary: Firebrand GOP Florida rep says party must prepare for difficult two years, says Republicans bear responsibility for loss as a team
articles.body: As Republicans sift through the wreckage of a devastating election night that handed Democrats control of both chambers of Congress by large margins, one Florida Republican who bucked the national trend says the GOP fundamentally misread the electorate. In an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital, Congressman Randy Fine — who expanded his own winning margin by five points despite the national backlash — offered a candid assessment of his party's shortcomings and warned that Republicans must now prepare for an "ugly two years" battling Democrats over immigration and other contentious issues. While Republicans held their ground in Florida, winning the governor's mansion, the Senate race, and maintaining their 20-8 edge in the US House, nationally the GOP got crushed under the weight of a blue tsunami. ILHAN OMAR HIT WITH EXPULSION THREAT AS GOP LAWMAKER VOWS TO BOOT HER FROM CONGRESS OVER DOJ PROBE Congressman Fine presents no easy answer to the GOP's divergence in fortunes between Florida and the rest of the country: "You know, I think that's a hard question to answer. What I would say, I can speak to my race, and I'm actually one of the few Republicans in the country whose margin increased from my last election. I won my special election after having $14 million spent against me. I won it by 14 points. I won last night by 19 points. And so what I can tell you is what worked for me. "My constituents want a fighter, someone who says what they believe. They know it's not driven by polls or anything else and fights for them, whether it's fighting for their constituent service issue or fighting on illegal immigration or fighting to bring money to the district. And that's why I went up so much. I took my race seriously because I knew the winds were against us. "And so, Florida, I think just people know how good we have it and they don't want to screw up the state. I think that's why we won all 20 of these races." Fine refuses to single out anyone in GOP leadership for the electoral outcome, and believes the Republicans must approach each election cycle as a unified team: "Well, look, I'm not a finger pointer, but what I would say is this. We're a team and the team lost. And so then the whole team bears responsibility and that includes me. I mean, while I did well, my team lost, and I'm not going to be here pointing the fingers at anybody. FROM CAMPUS RADICALS TO BEIJING'S AI SABOTAGE: REP RANDY FINE SAYS 'US FIGHTING TO SAVE WESTERN CIVILIZATION' "I think that what we did is we failed to understand what the American people wanted. I think we failed to make them think we cared about them. Now, I didn't fail in my district, but I think nationally people came to believe that we weren't interested in them and that's wrong. "We were, but we failed to communicate it, and maybe that's part of my special sauce is I know how to communicate better than many of these people." With Democrats firmly in control of both chambers of Congress, Fine anticipates two years of playing defense, and a continuous fight to explain why Democrats' policies will be harmful to the country: "I don't know that we're going to push the agenda. I think what we're going to be is we're going to be on defense. We're going to have to fight back. And you know, as my father told me this morning, he goes, 'Randy, you've been a fighter your whole life. You were built for the fight.' "So we're going to be having to fight against stupid policies that they will be pushing. And it's going to be an ugly two years, but we're gonna have to explain why all of the things that they said they would do during the campaign are so bad. We obviously didn't succeed in doing that. But as they put those policies forward, we're going to have to make the argument for why they would damage America." Immigration is the single issue that Fine identifies as having the greatest potential to harm the country: "I think they will seek to reopen the border and allow illegals to flood in. I think they will seek mass amnesty, rewarding all of the illegals that are here. And I think they will stop any requirement for people who come to this country to assimilate. They believe in the ‘third worldification’ of America. And that's going to be the number one thing we have to fight back against." Florida and Texas painted a particularly stark contrast in electoral outcomes. Fine suggests the Sunshine state GOP was better prepared to face headwinds: "Well, I think maybe our candidates at the top of the ticket were better. You know, Byron Donalds is an incredible spokesman for the conservative movement. Ashley Moody is a multiple-time winner statewide. And I think Texas allowed itself to slide on a lot of these things. "They had a big influx of illegal immigrants. And they also really didn't fight back against the Islamification of their state in a way that we have in Florida. Demographics are destiny. And I think, to some degree, Texas was overtaken by that yesterday." Fine has long been an outspoken critic of Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, and believes he represents a danger to the country: "Of all the races last night, that one breaks my heart the most. I mean, someone who literally supports Muslim terror, someone whose family is embedded in so many aspects of Muslim terror. Someone who's really a danger to this country being elected to the United States Senate. It's an unspeakably horrible thing, a historically bad thing. Someone who doesn't support the United States. Someone who supports the Muslim Brotherhood. "It breaks my heart. I'm not from Michigan, I don't know what they were thinking, but it's a terrible, terrible, terrible day. Look today for me has been a hard day. You know I won my election last night, I was super excited. My margin went up. It's unheard of in this cycle and so I'm super excited, then I watched the bottom fall out of the election results and realized so many good people lost today. "So it's a challenging day for me, the high of winning so decisively with the low of realizing the battle that we have ahead of us, but God puts us where he wants us to be and I'm a fighter and I am ready for the fight." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Finally, as it appears that either Jim Jordan or Steve Scalise is likely to be the next House Minority Leader, Fine declined to weigh in: "No, I mean, these are discussions. I've not spoken with either Scalise or Jordan at this point. They've got a lot of phone calls to make, and we'll get to that when we get to that. But it won't be Mike Johnson. He's taken himself out of consideration."

articles.title: Republicans quickly turn against Pete Hegseth after midterms rout
articles.summary: President Donald Trump may have made the decision to launch the war that tanked voters’ support for the GOP and dealt them a midterm shellacking. But the his...
articles.body:
President Donald Trump may have made the decision to launch the war that tanked voters' support for the GOP and dealt them a midterm shellacking. But the historic losses are accelerating a push for someone else to take the fall: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

And the House could vote as soon as next week to impeach the Pentagon's top leader.

Many Republican lawmakers and allies alarmed by Tuesday's wipeout are moving swiftly to pin blame for the election results on Hegseth, arguing behind the scenes that he played a chief role in convincing Trump to attack Iran with no exit strategy — and no plan for managing the inevitable political fallout.

The knives-out campaign comes despite private acknowledgement from House and Senate GOP strategists that the party's problems extended far beyond the war, triggering 2008-level losses that will take years to reverse. But for now, party leaders – and many in their ranks – remain unwilling to directly blame Trump for their woes.

Even among House Republicans who survived Tuesday's onslaught, there's zero expectation they will suddenly break from the president with two years left in his term. Yet that fealty does not extend to Hegseth, the combative defense secretary who has made few friends on Capitol Hill since taking over command of the Pentagon.

House Republicans are expected to vote to directly repudiate the defense secretary in a matter of days. Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, the famously anti-Trump GOP lawmaker, told CNN he plans to trigger a vote to impeach Hegseth when Congress returns next week — and multiple GOP sources said they expect it to pass.

Hegseth, a vocal cheerleader for the war, oversold the US' ability to win the conflict quickly and easily, multiple Republicans argued to CNN, describing on condition of anonymity why many in their party are now turning against the defense secretary. They accused him of continuing to advocate for escalation despite little sign that continued bombing has brought Iran closer to surrender.

The conflict has since turned into a quagmire, they said, entangling the US in the Middle East indefinitely, worsening the affordability crisis, and triggering voters' midterm revolt against the GOP. On Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance issued an extraordinary statement that "the reason we lost is the war," though he did not assign any specific blame for the conflict.

"The pivot is starting" on the war and Hegseth, a former senior Pentagon official said. "This has been primarily a Department of War-led effort because you chose to take military action to resolve a foreign policy matter."

Still, despite efforts around him to turn up the heat on Hegseth, Trump's own confidence in his defense secretary hasn't yet wavered even as he's continued to survey allies about his performance, multiple White House officials told CNN.

Trump personally likes Hegseth, and has told aides that he believes he should fight back against efforts to impeach him or launch investigations into his decision-making.

"Just two days ago the president was in the room with him, telling him, 'You're my best guy. You're the best guy I have,'" one of the officials said.

Trump may also feel an additional need to keep Hegseth around if he chooses to move forward with additional strikes against Iran, another source familiar with his thinking told CNN, especially with Democrats' new majority in the Senate likely to complicate any administration efforts to confirm new Cabinet appointees.

Pressed Wednesday on Hegseth's job status, Trump defended the war effort and denied any plans to fire him, saying he thought the defense secretary was "doing a very good job."

"If I had it to do again, I'd have to do it again," Trump said of his decision to go to war.

The White House also decried the prospect of Democratic investigations into the Pentagon, with spokeswoman Lauren Bis arguing in a statement that "if Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people."

But some Republicans feel it may be only a matter of time before Trump looks for someone to blame for the midterm losses, and they view Hegseth as an obvious target.

"If the president is serious about anyone taking responsibility for it, it's Pete Hegseth," one Republican close to the White House said of the electoral thrashing. "Pete has been either dishonest or incorrect — neither of which are acceptable — about timelines, goals and objectives since the beginning."

Trump has not yet signaled plans to fire any top officials. But in the aftermath of the GOP's midterm drubbing, allies and advisers widely expect him to eventually oversee some level of changes within the administration.

Within Trump's orbit, some have seized on Hegseth's likely impeachment as additional justification for making him the fall guy in the wake of an embarrassing rebuke of Trump's presidency — contending that he's bound to become a central target of Democrats' ire over the war anyway.

Hegseth, for his part, has been defiant about his ability to withstand the forthcoming wave of congressional scrutiny.

While he has at times discussed his potential future ambitions with allies — including possibly running for office in Tennessee — those closest to Trump don't believe that's an immediate goal of his, people familiar with the discussions said. (Some Republicans on the Hill, in the meantime, privately bristle at the prospect of Hegseth serving in Congress.)

In the immediate aftermath of Tuesday's midterm election results, one person close to Hegseth told CNN that Trump's defense secretary still expects to stay in his role and is prepared to fight an impeachment effort.

Hegseth has also communicated to the White House that he's prepared to own every policy decision and action taken by the Pentagon, the person said, believing that he's well-equipped to defend those moves in public hearings that would likely grow contentious if Democrats launch them after they take control of Congress in January.

In a statement, chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said that Hegseth "will not back down or be deterred by politicians seeking to score partisan points or launch phony investigations where no wrongdoing exists."

"We will continue to drive President Trump's agenda at the Department of War — despite threats of sham witch hunts from Democrats — and Secretary Hegseth is 100% committed to leading the Department until the end of President Trump's term in office," Parnell said.

Yet once that congressional scrutiny ramps up, Trump advisers and allies have questioned how long Hegseth's resolve might last. Even before Tuesday, several White House officials, members of the president's political operation and Trump allies candidly acknowledged the Iran war was — in their view — their biggest liability for the midterms. And Hegseth, one of the biggest proponents of military action in Iran, is intrinsically linked to that liability, they added.

"I think he probably knows he's dead but would like an exit sufficiently dramatic that it gives him a launching pad to run for POTUS," one administration official said.

For skeptics of the administration's open-ended war in Iran, successfully pushing Hegseth out of the Pentagon would mark a critical victory — but only the first step in a broader effort to bring the fight to an end.

After all, Massie noted, Trump has continued to argue for continuing the war in Iran, no matter the political and economic price paid at home.

"You don't screw up this badly an election with just one issue," Massie said. "It was completely avoidable if they'd just broken out of the cultish following of Donald Trump."

articles.title: Mississippi Senate race heads to an extended vote count and possible ballot battle
articles.summary: The Mississippi Senate race may take days to resolve, as Democrat Scott Colom leads GOP Sen.
articles.body: The Mississippi Senate race may take days to resolve, as Democrat Scott Colom leads GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by just 65 votes in the current vote count. And as votes continue to be counted, all eyes are on an unknown number of ballots that could shift the result — and lead to a very murky recount process. Mississippi has not been a site of close vote counts and postelection drama in recent years. But Colom’s strong showing comes as Democrats swept several Senate races in red states across the country. While Democrats have a Senate majority without flipping Mississippi, it could be their reddest pickup. And it would be another victory in a string of wins in the South, including in Texas and South Carolina, after years of struggle for Democrats. National operatives are descending on the state, with staff members from the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and the Elias Law Group on the ground Wednesday to lead the Democratic effort to ensure votes are counted, according to a source familiar with the effort, who was granted anonymity to discuss legal strategy. A partner with the Elias Law Group, which has served as the Colom campaign’s lawyers, told NBC News they were heading to Mississippi to investigate the outstanding vote. Colom, a local prosecutor, said at a news conference Wednesday morning: “We’re prepared to litigate, though we were prepared for this for months. We have an army of lawyers. We have local lawyers. We have everybody involved to make sure the process is followed according to the law.” Colom and Hyde-Smith’s campaign manager, Jake Monssen, both said Wednesday that there are “thousands” of outstanding ballots. But the exact number remains unclear. Around 6,000 mail ballots appear to have been distributed but not yet been returned Monday, according to data from the Mississippi secretary of state’s office, which did not reply to a request for comment. Mail ballots postmarked by Election Day can be counted in Mississippi if they are received by 5 p.m. Nov. 10. An unknown number of so-called affidavit ballots, also known as provisional ballots, are also outstanding. Those were issued to voters who do not have the proper ID or are not on the list of registered voters. Mikell Bolden, the Mississippi Democratic Party’s executive director, said in a phone interview Wednesday that the party’s election hotline received around 2,000 calls Tuesday from across the state, many of them from voters who were told they had to cast affidavit ballots. Voters said they were certain they were registered to vote, Bolden said, but were told they were not on the voter roll when they went to cast their ballots. And Bolden said those voters could not check their own registration status, because the secretary of state’s website had crashed. Bolden said the state party, the Colom campaign and the national party are working to reach out to voters via phone calls, text messages and robocalls to ensure those who were affected return their ballots or address issues related to their affidavit ballots, like showing the proper ID, by Tuesday, which would allow them to be counted. “Everything is on the line right now for this state,” Bolden said. And it will be a weeklong scramble — county election officials must transmit the election results to the secretary of state by Nov. 13. Republicans are also signaling that they are gearing up for a legal fight. Hyde-Smith campaign manager Jake Monssen said in a statement Wednesday that the campaign is “closely monitoring the remaining count” and is confident she will prevail. Joanna Rodriguez, a National Republican Senatorial Committee spokeswoman, told NBC News in a statement, “As the democratic process continues to play out, we are committed to ensuring that every single lawful ballot is accurately counted and the voice of all Mississippians is heard.” While the focus is on the outstanding ballots, there are also new questions about a potential recount. Ben Griffith, a voting rights and election law attorney who teaches at the University of Mississippi, told NBC News the options for Colom or Hyde-Smith to challenge the results are limited. There is no mechanism for an election to undergo a recount under Mississippi state law. There is also no mechanism for a U.S. Senate general election race to be otherwise contested, according to state law and the Mississippi election handbook. Candidates can challenge the results county by county by filing their intentions with particular county clerks to “examine” the contents of the counties’ ballot box. But with 82 counties across the state and nine days until the canvassing must be complete, “that’s beyond the scope of feasibility,” Griffith said. There are avenues for candidates in local elections across the state to challenge results of particular races with the Legislature — but not the U.S. Senate race.

articles.title: Midterm defeat deals death blow to Trump coalition
articles.summary: Commentators argued that the Democratic rout spells the end of US President Donald Trump’s political movement.
articles.body:
A historic Democratic rout sounded the death knell for the Trump coalition, commentators argued.

Republicans' midterm wipeout on Tuesday marks the end of a nationalist movement based on " projecting invulnerability and ruthlessness ," Politico wrote, to which "so many executives and diplomats and generals and prime ministers chose to submit."

Still, the results don't guarantee years of Democratic dominance: Swing voters are " leasing one-year terms ," journalist Derek Thompson wrote, making Tuesday less a realignment than a "historic collapse."

President Donald Trump's once-successful strategy of turning out his base "with money from people who didn't understand that base" didn't work this time, Semafor's David Weigel argued: "Democrats made a bet that gravity was real, and Trump couldn't defy it anymore ."

articles.title: Democrats' 2026 midterm rout was big — really big. Here are the numbers that prove it.
articles.summary: The last time either party won the House midterm vote by at least 13 points was right after Watergate.
articles.body:
Midterms tend to be backlash elections, and the president's party almost always loses seats when voters return to the polls to judge his performance in office.

On Tuesday, Democrats comprehensively routed their Republican rivals , regaining control of the U.S. House, U.S. Senate and statehouses across the country. Along the way, they shattered a series of decades-long Republican winning streaks and notched several historic firsts .

So just how big was this year's blue wave (or " blue tsunami ")?

The full scale and scope of the Democratic Party's seismic victory is still coming into focus as officials tally every last vote. But here are some key numbers to help you put it into perspective:

26: the average number of House seats the president's party has lost in midterm elections since World War II (pre-2026)

40+: the projected number of House seats that will flip to Democrats in 2026, once all the votes are counted

About 255: the projected size of the new Democratic House majority — the largest since 2008, and possibly since 1992

6.8 percentage points: the Republican popular vote margin in their 1994 and 2010 House midterm victories

13 points: the projected Democratic popular vote margin in their 2026 House midterm victory

1974: the last time either party won their House popular vote by that much in a midterm election

More than 100: the number of Democratic women who will serve simultaneously in the House — a historic first

4: the average number of Senate seats the president's party has lost in midterm elections since World War II (pre-2026)

9: the number of Republican Senate seats that have either flipped to Democrats in 2026 (Iowa, Kansas, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina, Texas) or could flip once all the votes are counted (Alaska, Mississippi)

55-56: the projected size of the new Democratic Senate majority — the largest since the early 2010s

2014: the last time a party — the Republicans — flipped 9 Senate seats in a midterm election

1958: the last time a party flipped more than 9 Senate seats in a midterm election

12 points: Trump's average margin of victory in 2024 in the nine states where Democrats flipped or could still flip a Republican Senate seat this year

1986: The last midterm in which more than two Senate seats flipped in states where the president won by double-digit margins two years earlier

At least 17: the number of senators from both parties who will be replaced in the chamber after the 2026 midterms — the largest turnover since 1980

70: the average age of this year's departing senators

At least 15: the number of senators from both parties who will be under 50 when they're sworn into office in January 2027 — up from eight previously

7: the number of Republican governorships that have either flipped to Democrats in 2026 (Iowa, Ohio, Georgia, Nevada, Texas) or could flip once all the votes are counted (Alaska, Kansas)

As many as 31: the number of governorships that Democrats could control once all the votes are counted

2011: The last time Democrats controlled a majority of governorships

About 75%: the percentage of Americans who will live in states with Democratic governors after the 2026 midterms

63%: the percentage of exit poll respondents who said they disapprove of how Trump is handling his job as president

54%: the percentage of exit poll respondents who said they "strongly" disapprove of how Trump is handling his job as president

37%: the percentage of exit poll respondents who said they approve of how Trump is handling his job as president — the lowest midterm approval of any president since at least 2006

91%: the percentage of exit poll respondents who said government corruption was a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress

62%: the percentage of exit poll respondents who said Trump prioritizes his own personal interests over the country's interests

89%: the percentage of exit poll respondents who said the cost of living was a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress

66%: the percentage of exit poll respondents who said Trump's policies have worsened economic conditions in the U.S.

+15 percentage points: An early estimate of how much better Democrats performed nationwide in 2026 vs. 2024 (via the New York Times )

+20 points: An early estimate of how much better Democrats performed in the South in 2026 vs. 2024

+28 points: An early estimate of how much better Democrats performed with Latino voters in 2026

+32 points: An early estimate of much better Democrats performed with young voters (ages 18-29) in 2026 vs. 2024

2.6 percentage points: Democrat James Talarico's final lead in the polls, on average

About 12 points: Talarico's actual margin of victory over Republican Ken Paxton in the 2026 midterm election

1988: The last time Texas elected a Democratic senator

5.26 million: The number of votes Joe Biden received in Texas in the 2020 presidential election

5.45 million: The number of votes Talarico has received in Texas in the 2026 midterm election — the most ever for a Democrat

64%: The estimated percentage of Texas independent voters that Talarico won in the 2026 midterm election

70%: The estimated percentage of Texas Latino voters that Talarico won in the 2026 midterm election

73%: The estimated percentage of young voters (ages 18-29) that Talarico won in the 2026 midterm election

articles.summary: Hallie Jackson, Garrett Haake and Ryan Nobles discuss a historic night of Democratic victories.
articles.body: Welcome to the daily Inside Scoop newsletter. It was a huge night for Democrats, who forced a realignment of the congressional map with historic wins in Republican strongholds. How did they succeed? And what comes next? “Hallie Jackson NOW” host Hallie Jackson, chief White House correspondent Garrett Haake and chief Capitol Hill correspondent Ryan Nobles joined me on today’s “Here’s the Scoop” podcast for a comprehensive panel discussion. Let’s get into it. Democrats will reclaim the House and Senate majorities, NBC News projects, doing so with victories in Texas, Ohio, Kansas, Iowa and other states that Donald Trump won by double digits in 2024.
